title: Your BMI Says You're Healthy — a Landmark Study Says Millions Aren't, and South Asians Are Most at Risk
excerpt: A quarter of Americans with a 'normal' BMI already meet the clinical standard for obesity, and the blind spot is even wider for people of South Asian descent
body:
Your doctor's scale says you're fine. A landmark study says it may be lying.

New research from Keck Medicine of USC, published in the *Annals of Internal Medicine*, has found that body mass index — the height-and-weight formula that has defined obesity screening for decades — dramatically underestimates who actually carries dangerous levels of body fat. A quarter of people with a "normal" BMI, the study found, already meet the newer clinical standard for obesity. Among those labeled merely "overweight," fully half would be reclassified as obese.

The implications ripple outward from doctor's offices to insurance approvals: people who do not register as obese on a BMI chart currently cannot qualify for GLP-1 medications, bariatric surgery, or targeted lifestyle intervention programs. Millions may be accruing obesity-related damage to their hearts, livers, and joints without anyone flagging the risk.

"Many people assume that if their BMI says they are not obese, they don't have to worry about the many health problems linked to obesity," said Brian P. Lee, a hepatologist at Keck Medicine and the study's principal investigator. "Our findings show that millions of Americans may already have obesity-related health impacts and may be missing needed health interventions."

## Why BMI misses so much

BMI divides weight by the square of height. It does not distinguish between muscle, bone, water, and fat — or, critically, *where* fat sits on the body. A muscular athlete can register as overweight while a sedentary office worker with dangerous visceral fat slips through as normal.

The USC team studied more than 5,600 participants from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), comparing their BMI readings against waist circumference, waist-to-hip ratio, and waist-to-height ratio — measures that capture abdominal fat, the kind most tightly linked to heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and fatty liver.

Their conclusion: the newer "clinical obesity" framework, which combines abdominal fat measurements with weight-related health markers, catches a far larger population at genuine metabolic risk. If the United States were to screen using waist-based ratios alongside BMI, the adult obesity rate would jump from the CDC's current 40 percent estimate to roughly 75 percent, according to a related December 2025 JAMA analysis.

## A warning that hits South Asians hardest

For the Indian diaspora, the BMI blind spot is not merely an American health policy curiosity — it is personal. Decades of research, including the landmark MASALA study of South Asian Americans, have shown that people of South Asian descent develop type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic syndrome at BMI levels well below the standard thresholds. The WHO has long recommended lower cut-offs for Asian populations: overweight at a BMI of 23 rather than 25, and obesity at 25 rather than 30.

Yet these adjusted thresholds are rarely used in clinical practice in the United States, Canada, or the United Kingdom. A South Asian American man with a BMI of 26 — officially just "overweight" — may already be carrying the visceral fat profile of a clinically obese individual.

The phenomenon is sometimes called the "thin-fat" phenotype: lower overall body weight but higher proportions of visceral and ectopic fat deposited around the liver, pancreas, and skeletal muscle. The MASALA study found that South Asians had greater intermuscular fat, lower lean muscle mass, and more unfavorable adipokine profiles than every other ethnic group studied, even at comparable BMIs.

"South Asians exhaust the storage capacity of subcutaneous fat compartments before other populations do," researchers have noted, "resulting in metabolic complications at lower absolute masses of adipose tissue."

## What this means for NRIs

For NRIs relying on annual physicals that use BMI as the primary screen, the message is straightforward: ask for a waist circumference measurement. A tape measure costs nothing and takes seconds, yet captures metabolic risk that a scale alone misses entirely.

The American Diabetes Association now recommends screening South Asian Americans for type 2 diabetes starting at a BMI of 23 — seven points lower than the general-population threshold of 30. Knowing that number, and insisting on ethnic-specific screening, could mean catching prediabetes years before it becomes irreversible.

"The good news is that obesity can be treated," Lee said. "Whether through lifestyle changes, medication, or both, we have effective ways to reduce excess body fat and lower the risk of future health problems. The earlier we identify people at risk, the better chance we have of improving long-term health and quality of life."

The study adds to a growing consensus: BMI was a useful shortcut for population-level estimates. For individual diagnosis — and especially for the 32 million members of the global Indian diaspora — it was never enough.

---

*Sources: Annals of Internal Medicine (June 2026), Keck Medicine of USC, JAMA (December 2025), MASALA Study / MESA, WHO Expert Consultation on Asian BMI Thresholds*
